checks: Read both author pages in full, including the immediately preceding general reference to plants newly covered by BEHG, the following hazardous-waste sentences, and the alternative request for a targeted exemption or suspension of BEHG.

Independently read the Danish Energy Agency original release of 28 May 2014, Danish Tax Agency guidance 2026-1 for waste incineration, the Swedish government directive of 2 June 2016 at its ETS section, and the relevant Danish/Swedish/Norwegian portions of the Nordic 2024 governmental report. These affirm foreign pricing of waste-to-energy installations.

Read the archived January EHV consultation draft cover and problem/solution section, and operative section 4 beginning at printed page 20. The request concerns the wider underlying market rather than a claim that this implementing draft first imposed waste pricing.
analysis: The general wording creates a worthwhile lead, and absence of a uniform European obligation does not entail absence of all foreign carbon costs. Nevertheless, the immediately preceding reference to newly BEHG-covered plants can delimit the following demonstrative to a specific cohort. The ensuing substantive discussion and requested exemption concern hazardous-waste installations. Affirmative foreign examples are principally energy-recovery installations. The Swedish government expressly distinguishes energy-production purpose from waste-destruction purpose, while Danish guidance excludes dedicated hazardous/municipal-waste facilities from ETS. Those are substantive scope differences, not merely missing data. No matched hazardous/dedicated-waste counterexample is established here.
strongest_alternative: The author may mean the additional German charge for the cohort newly entering BEHG, particularly dedicated hazardous-waste sites, rather than all installations that burn waste anywhere. A separate instrument-specific reading is also possible, although the causal appeal to European coverage makes that reading less complete.
materiality: Potentially minor if the broad generic reading were established: foreign counterexamples would qualify uniqueness but not equalize coverage or costs. At present the interpretation uncertainty precedes materiality adjudication.
direction: Null while unresolved. Under the broad reading a Germany-only claim would support the requested exemption or suspension, but direction cannot resolve which cohort the author meant.
limits: Do not infer that the printed Germany-only statement is correct. This review withholds a proved-error finding because the presently established foreign counterexamples may concern a different legal cohort.
Do not claim equal net costs, identical coverage, or pricing of hazardous waste in the foreign examples. No policy merit or intent conclusion follows.
A matched foreign dedicated-waste carbon charge applicable by 29 January 2026, or an explicit broader scope clarification in the author record, could resolve this lead.

new_primary_reads: Independently read the complete Danish Tax Agency2026-1 E.A.4.2.1 historical/operative overview: the hazardous-waste subsection expressly identifies CO2 tax from1January2015, and the immediately following ETS subsection separately excludes hazardous incineration from ETS. This is affirmative carbon-tax coverage, not inference from ordinary energy-recovery ETS plants.

Read the non-ETS calculation and exemption discussion in2026-1 E.A.4.5.7.3, including heat/electricity treatment, qualifying waste, and exceptions. Pure destruction without taxable energy use and eligible exempt material must not be described as universally charged.

Read the relevant Danish parliamentary ministerial2022 answer identifying Fortum as a specialised hazardous-waste incineration/destruction facility. It corroborates existence of the dedicated cohort; its proposed future rates are not treated as paid charges.
follow_up.reassessment: The original objection depended on counterexamples being only an unrelated energy-recovery ETS cohort. The new official guidance expressly establishes a separate hazardous-incineration carbon-tax regime, including plants outside ETS. A general claim that waste-incineration carbon costs arise exclusively in Germany is therefore overstated even under a hazardous-waste-focused reading. We do not need to establish tax on every dedicated destruction plant to refute a universal exclusive-country description. Nevertheless, instrument-specific additional German costs and particular unpriced destruction operations remain material qualifications.
follow_up.materiality: Retain minor only: the correction qualifies international uniqueness, not competitive parity or the appropriateness of suspension/exemption. No current operator-specific amount or net fiscal burden is established.

limits: Retain heat/energy-use and non-biodegradable-waste scope, national instrument differences, exemptions, cost pass-through and possible compensation. No claim of identical German/Danish legal scope or net costs.
The official guide describes a historical rule still in force in its2026-1 text. No full tax-law consolidation audit or professionally certified Danish translation is claimed.
If the raw record remains framed as all hazardous plants necessarily charged abroad, that broader wording is not supported by this review.
